speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: asked the Prime Minister (a) what is the aggregate dollar value of the subject matter of corruption cases investigated or prosecuted in 2020; (b) how much has been seized or forfeited as proceeds of corruption for the same year; (c) how do both figures compare with the preceding two years’ figures; and (d) what steps have CPIB identified to beef up its digital capabilities in the fight against corruption and to deal with operational issues during the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Corruption is not tolerated in any form in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: It undermines public trust and erodes our social fabric.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: It pursues all corruption cases regardless of the types of gratification, the quantum of the contracts or amount of bribes involved.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Singapore has a hard-won international reputation as a country committed to the rule of law and zero tolerance for corruption.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The strong political will to take firm action against all forms of corruption and a society that abhors corruption have contributed to a clean and incorruptible Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Businesses have the confidence that their investments can thrive here because our rules are transparent and applied fairly.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Singaporeans can fulfil their potential through their own efforts and hard work in our meritocratic society.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Corrupt offenders bear the full brunt of the law and face severe punishments.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: In addition, CPIB spares no effort to disgorge criminal gains and unexplained assets of those convicted of corruption offences through its rigorous asset recovery efforts.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Some examples include the Electronic Reporting of Corruption Complaints and the Electronic Bail platform which provides bailors and bailees with safe and convenient access to bail extension services virtually.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: CPIB also launched a Digital Investigation Paper project where documents can be digitally and securely prepared, transmitted and accessed.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: CPIB will continue to take bold steps to transform itself and develop its operational readiness to meet emerging challenges in a post-COVID-19 future.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: To stay ahead of the curve, CPIB has invested in state-of-the-art digital infrastructure through collaboration with strategic partners such as the Home Team Science and Technology Agency and other agencies.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: In the prevention and outreach arena, CPIB has co-created public education resources with students from Institutes of Higher Learning such as Nanyang Polytechnic, and schools such as St Joseph’s Institution.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Some initiatives include an e-book on actual corruption cases and its consequences on the society and a Game Web Application incorporating anti-corruption materials for young adults.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Singapore's clean and corruption-free reputation should not be taken for granted as it is not immune to the virus of corruption.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Singapore must keep fighting corruption wherever it exists and in whatever form it takes.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: There is no room for complacency and it requires the constant vigilance and resolute determination of the Government, the Public Service and the community to continue to keep corruption at bay.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Hon Members would have also read CPIB's annual report 2020, which was presented to Parliament on 21 April 2021.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The work to detect and investigate cases of corruption is complex.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In most crime cases, there will be an identifiable victim; for example, a person who has been cheated of his monies or whose valuables have been stolen.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For corruption, the paradigm is different; not a win-lose situation but a win-win situation involving the giver and the acceptor of bribes.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As a result of its work and the support of Singaporeans, Singapore has established a strong brand and culture of being intolerant of corruption.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Singapore, Singaporean businesses and Singaporeans enjoy a good reputation overseas for the same reason.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For this, all of us in this House owe the men and women of CPIB, past and present, a debt of gratitude.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Next, may I seek an update, if any, on the hon Minister's announcement recently that the legislative levers the CPIB uses, in particular, the Prevention of Corruption Act, are being reviewed to keep them relevant in the fight against corruption?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Indeed, for the past 69 years, CPIB has been unwavering and relentless in its efforts to fight corruption.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Other than the political will to fight corruption, heavy punishments and effective anti-corruption laws, as well as public support are all very important factors contributing to the low corruption in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: While the Prevention of Corruption Act (PCA) has and continues to serve us well, CPIB will regularly and proactively review the provisions to make sure that the Act is able to keep pace with, if not, stay ahead of the evolving threats.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: To the Member's question, I can share the following areas which CPIB is working on with respect to the PCA review.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Indeed, we must not let our guard down.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Likewise, low corruption does not mean no corruption.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Corruption if embedded and becomes endemic in our society will alter the fundamental DNA of our societal ethos that has been painstakingly built up over the past many decades.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This threat will then diminish the trust and confidence that Singaporeans and others have in one another and in our system, eroding the work ethics and tearing our social fabric apart.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, to Mr Murali's comment, yes, indeed, in some of these corruption cases, it is a win-win situation for the person providing the bribes and for the person receiving the bribes.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But the victims are actually the whole society and our own ethos of what we stand for as a nation and as a people.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The damage goes beyond what may be transacted between the two perpetrators.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is why while CPIB has done well in its work all these years, as a society, we need to maintain our vigilance.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The threat is always evolving, especially with technological advances and evolving corrupt practices.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It is thus important to ensure that the DNA of incorruptibility is ingrained in every Singaporean, young and old.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: CPIB has been educating our youths and working with them to co-create public education resources for the youths, by the youths.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Some of these initiatives were mentioned in my earlier response.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Our people must always believe that they can succeed because of their honest and hard work.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This brand of incorruptibility is also what allows Singapore and Singaporeans to stand tall amidst the global competition, even beyond our shores.
